title: British man infected with Ebola in DR Congo to be flown back to UK
description: A British man who has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo will be flown back to the UK.It is the first confirmed case of a U
body: A British man who has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo will be flown back to the UK.It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.It is not clear when the flight will take place.Earlier, a UK government spokesperson said there were "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and that the risk to the public remains low.Reuters news agency reported the infected man is a healthcare worker, citing an internal document BBC News has not seen.Imported Ebola cases are extremely rare in the UK and have resulted in no deaths.There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK - one, in 1976, resulting from a laboratory incident, and three involving health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.A UK government spokesperson said: "The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated."Further information will be shared in due course as appropriate. The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low."There have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases since the recent outbreak in DR Congo started in May, which has grown to become the second most deadly recorded spate of infections, behind the outbreak in West Africa.It has since become the deadliest in the country's history, with a fatality rate of 48.6% reported at the end of last month.

schema.headline: British man infected with Ebola in DR Congo to be flown back to UK

title: Cocaine overtakes heroin as leading cause of drug deaths in England and Wales
description: The number of deaths from cocaine use in England and Wales has nearly quadrupled in a decade, overtaking those attributed to heroin for the first time
body: The number of deaths from cocaine use in England and Wales has nearly quadrupled in a decade, overtaking those attributed to heroin for the first time.Cocaine was linked to more than one in five drug poisoning deaths registered in 2025, more than any other single substance, with charities blaming its increased purity and availability.Meanwhile a record 115 ketamine-linked deaths were registered, almost twice as many as in 2024, according to Office for National Statistics data, external.The overall rate of drug deaths fell for the first time since 2012. But experts pointed out regional inequality was growing, with the rate of such deaths more than twice as high in the North East as in London.There were 5,519 drug poisoning deaths registered in 2025 in England and Wales, the equivalent of 92.4 deaths per million people.Of these, cocaine was mentioned in 1,233 cases - slightly fewer than the previous year but higher than the 1,210 deaths linked to heroin or morphine, which also marked a fall from the previous year's level.However, deaths linked to opiate and opioid drugs combined were still higher. The ONS also said there was a lag between deaths occurring and being registered.The fatality rate fell from 93.9 deaths per million people a year earlier, representing the first annual decline since 2012.In September, National Records of Scotland said drug deaths there had risen by 11% in 2025 on the year before, marking the worst mortality rate in Europe, In May the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency said drug-related deaths rose by 7.1% between 2021-23 and 2022-24, external.

schema.headline: Cocaine overtakes heroin as leading cause of drug deaths in England and Wales

title: Zelensky gives Melania Trump Ukraine's highest award after Oleshky ceasefire
description: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has given the country's highest award for women to the US First Lady, Melania Trump. The Order of Princess Olha
body: Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has given the country's highest award for women to the US First Lady, Melania Trump. The Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, was awarded to Melania Trump for her "significant personal contribution to humanitarian support for Ukraine", according to the presidential decree. It comes after the end of ceasefire in Ukraine's southern region of Kherson, which allowed for the evacuation of several hundred people from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. Russian and Ukrainian delegations - made up of ombudsmen who were involved in the evacuation mission as well as senior officials - are due to meet at the White House on Thursday on Melania Trump's invitation.The White House said that Melania Trump had "independently initiated engagement between the two warring nations and successfully secured a ceasefire"."This achievement marks an unprecedented diplomatic initiative by an American First Lady", it added.Both the Russian and Ukrainian sides repeatedly thanked Melania Trump for brokering the ceasefire, though neither elaborated on the nature or extent of her involvement.The delegations travelling to the White House on Thursday will include Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and his Russian counterpart Yana Lantratova, as well as Ukrainian MP Davyd Arakhamia and Russian senior official Kirill Dmitriev. Lubinets and Lantratova travelled together into Oleshky last week, in an unusual show of cooperation between Russian and Ukrainian officials. Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads Zelensky's party in parliament, has previously been part of the Ukrainian negotiating team during peace talks with Russia. He was responsible for informal contact between the White House and Moscow during the ceasefire, according to diplomatic sources quoted by Ukrainian media, and has confirmed he will take part in Thursday's talks.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Russian delegation will be made up of Lantratova and Kirill Dmitriev, a Russian businessman close to the Kremlin who has frequently taken part in US-brokered ceasefire talks. Dmitriev and Arakhamia are veteran participants in high-level peace negotiations, and it is unusual for meetings involving such senior representatives to be convened through an initiative led by a US First Lady.No details of what the White House event will entail have been shared. "There are important meetings ahead," said Lubinets in a social media post while announcing he was on his way to the US.On Thursday Melania Trump will also deliver remarks on the ceasefire in Oleshky at 11:00 (16:00 GMT), the White House website said.Zelensky's decree also cited Melania Trump's wider humanitarian work, including her efforts concerning Ukrainian children affected by the war, as reasons for giving her the Princess Olga award. Melania Trump has largely remained discreet on foreign policy matters, but in 2025 she said an "open channel of communication" had been established with Russian President Vladimir Putin, allowing for Ukrainian children displaced in the war to be reunited with families.Earlier this year the UN said the deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia constitutes a crime against humanity and a war crime. According to Ukraine, almost 20,000 children have been illegally sent to Russia and Belarus since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Russian, Ukrainian and American representatives are also going to meet in Abu Dhabi next week in the first trilateral meeting since February. The talks will be focused on postwar security agreements and de-escalation, US envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.

schema.headline: Zelensky gives Melania Trump Ukraine's highest award after Oleshky ceasefire

title: Fewer mothers to appear in court days after giving birth under new guidance
description: The number of mothers going to court for child care proceedings within hours or days of giving birth will be reduced after new guidance was issued to
body: The number of mothers going to court for child care proceedings within hours or days of giving birth will be reduced after new guidance was issued to judges.The changes follow concerns about the increasing number of urgent applications brought to family courts for newborn babies where there is a safeguarding concern.A recent BBC investigation highlighted the issue after hearing of the traumatic experience for mothers having to attend court while recovering from labour.Under the new guidance issued by the Judiciary, same-day hearings should only be granted if a child's immediate safety is at risk to ensure intervention is "focused on cases that genuinely require it".In October, the BBC reported the number of children involved in care proceedings before they reached their first birthdays was at a persistently high level across England, based on research from the universities of Lancaster and Oxford.More than half of urgent care hearings in England in 2024-25 were for newborns, where mothers had to attend court within days of giving birth, or even potentially on the same day.While there are cases where it is unsafe for parents to continue contact with their children, experts told the BBC's File on 4 Investigates that many babies may not have needed to go into care if support had been in place.Since very young children who go into care are more likely to be adopted than older children, there are concerns from experts that some may have been permanently separated from their birth families unnecessarily.Following a consultation, new guidance instructs courts to be rigorous in refusing to deal with cases that do not meet the criteria of urgency.The expectation is that it would be extremely rare for an application to be made for a same-day hearing, the new guidance states.It outlines that a same-day hearing should only be sought if a child's "immediate safety" would be compromised without the court's intervention.Research from the Nuffield Family Justice Observatory found that over 70% of care proceedings involving babies in England were emergency hearings within two days of an application being made.Emma Smale, its head of practice and policy, described the new guidance as a "welcome focus" on the issue.She said the number of newborn babies in care proceedings in England and Wales subject to a same day hearing had doubled over a decade - from one in 10 in 2012-13 to one in five in 2022-23. Smale said the process of separating a mother from their baby when they have just given birth is "widely accepted as deeply traumatic for all involved", and called into question the fairness of making "profoundly life-changing decisions" when a parent cannot effectively participate in the proceedings.Under the new guidance, applicants for emergency or short notice listings - which take place within five days - will be required to justify with evidence why a case needs such a listing.If a judge does not agree with the level of urgency, the case will be given a standard listing between days 12 and 18.The Judiciary said the guidance is intended to help ensure parents and guardians "have time to respond more effectively to the application" and urgent judicial intervention is "focused on cases that genuinely require it".A Newborn Baby Protocol has also been issued, which aims to provide a "greater level of fairness for child and parents" when care proceedings are issued immediately after the child's birth.In England, early referral and assessment by local authority children's services will ensure the "timely provision" of preventative help, which should include identifying and strengthening family network resources, where this is in the child's best interests.The protocol also states that before making any care order application, a Family Group Decision Making Meeting must be offered to parents, in line with the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026.

schema.headline: Fewer mothers to appear in court days after giving birth under new guidance

title: Brigitte Bardot inheritance row deepens after private letter to partner leaked
description: A row over the inheritance of late screen legend Brigitte Bardot has intensified after a private letter was made public which appears to show her cutt
body: A row over the inheritance of late screen legend Brigitte Bardot has intensified after a private letter was made public which appears to show her cutting off relations with her last partner.Dated November 2022 – three years before she died at her home in Saint Tropez – the hand-written note accuses Bernard de Chiara, her companion of more than 30 years, of "patiently destroying me day after day".The leaked letter is a useful weapon for the other side in the Bardot legacy battle - the animal rights foundation that bears her name - which is accused by de Chiara of rushing to dispose of her estate without regard for friends and intimates.A week ago de Chiara, who is 85, was forced to leave the seaside house known as La Madrague which he shared with Bardot from the early 1990s. After being looked after financially by her for so many years, he is reported to possess neither a bank account nor a social security card.He was also furious after the Brigitte Bardot Foundation organised a sale in September of household objects mainly taken from the late actress's Paris flat. The sale raised nearly €1m (£835,000), shared between the Foundation and Bardot's only son Nicolas Charrier."I found it extraordinary that just a few months after Brigitte's death, they already wanted to make a souvenir out of her. I did not appreciate that one bit," de Chiara said.In the letter, which begins "Bernard, it's a failure!", Bardot said she had given "everything" in the hope of finding a "companion would could offer back my love, share my joys and immense sorrows... who is happy at the life I am giving him."But she concluded: "Today I have reached the end-point of my distress... I am so in need of a shoulder, a support, a tenderness, a presence – which you are incapable of giving."Widely known under the adopted name d'Ormale (a pun on the French dort mal – sleeps badly), de Chiara was a businessman and one-time associate of far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen.Friends say that he and Bardot had an up-and-down relationship. They were never married under French law, but he was living with her to the end and cared for her as she was dying.When her will was read after her death last December, it divided the estate between the Foundation and her son, who lives discreetly in Oslo. There was no mention of de Chiara, and Bardot also stipulated that La Madrague should be unoccupied within six months of her death.As lawyers now draw up a definitive list of the late actresses' assets, the Foundation accused de Chiara of removing items from La Madrague, including her Mini Moke jeep. "I am not accusing him of theft, but it's gone and that's a problem," said Foundation President Max Guazzani on Tuesday.According to the Foundation, de Chiara has no legal claim except for a share of the Paris flat, which is now up for sale. In the meantime he is living in an apartment rented from the town hall of Saint Tropez.Guazzini said that "on a human level one can understand [de Chiara's reluctance to leave La Madrague]. But it's the law and it's also what Brigitte Bardot wanted."It's not our fault that she did not leave him the right to live there. What else are we supposed to do?"The high cost of maintaining La Madrague – and Bardot's second home La Garrigue in the hills behind the Mediterranean coast – means the Foundation needs to find ways to make the properties pay. Both houses were in a poor state when she died, and now need round-the-clock security.An idea for a museum has been abandoned because La Madrague is inaccessible by car. Instead the house could be opened up for guided tours, as well as for fashion displays and film shoots.After Bardot left the world of cinema in 1973 she devoted her life to animal welfare and her foundation says it now cares for 13,000 animals.Bardot was married three times before she met de Chiara: to filmmaker Roger Vadim, actor Jacques Charrier and industrial heir Gunter Sachs.French media say she married de Chiara at a ceremony in Norway but this was never registered in French law.

schema.headline: Brigitte Bardot inheritance row deepens after private letter to partner leaked

title: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing
description: The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukr
body: The bodycam footage was released by Ukraine's national police on Wednesday.It shows huge devastation after the first bomb strike on the village in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region, as shocked local residents stare at the rubble.Severely damaged buildings are also seen.A voice of a military official is then heard on a two-way radio warning police on the ground of more glide bombs being launched towards Kamyshuvakha."Quickly [go] to the shelter!" one of the police officers tells local residents, who are seen walking into the shelter - at least two floors underground.Seconds later the shelter is hit, and the recording stops. Ukraine said the shelter was near a local school, which was being used to distribute humanitarian aid.BBC Verify has confirmed the video was filmed in the same place as footage released by the Ukrainian state emergencies service DSNS showing the aftermath Monday's attack in Komyshuvakha.In a post on social media on Wednesday, Zelensky said that "nine aerial bombs were dropped by the Russians. "First, they hit people who came to receive humanitarian aid, and then rescuers and police officers who arrived at the scene."The Ukrainian president added that "unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack", describing it as yet another of "thousands" of war crimes committed by Russia.Ukraine's DSNS earlier posted another video showing a huge crater left after the attack on Kamyshuvakha.The Russian military has not publicly commented.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.In a separate development on Wednesday, Zelensky said he talked "in great detail for an hour-and-a-half" with US President Donald Trump's peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of trilateral negotiations between Ukraine, Russia and the US on 10-11 November in Abu-Dhabi.The Ukrainian leader - who is currently making a surprise visit to Spain - also said his team had a separate "meaningful" meeting in Brussels with representatives from the US, the EU, France, Britain, Germany, as well as Nato and the World Bank about "post-war reconstruction".He added that the meeting in Belgium's capital would continue on Thursday to discuss "security guarantees" for Ukraine.Since the trilateral talks aimed at ending the war were suspended in February, Moscow has stepped up attacks as Kyiv virtually ran out of Western-supplied interceptors to defend against missiles.Analysts expect no major breakthrough when the talks resume in the capital of the United Arab Emirates.  Additional reporting Paul Brown, BBC Verify

schema.headline: Ukraine says bodycam video shows deadly Russian double-tap bombing

title: UK government to outlaw new North Sea drilling
description: Image caption, The new law would not affect the decision on whether to start production at the Rosebank site ByAngus CochraneSenior political journali
body: Image caption, The new law would not affect the decision on whether to start production at the Rosebank site ByAngus CochraneSenior political journalist, BBC ScotlandThe UK government has moved to ban any new exploration for oil and gas in the North Sea. The Energy Independence Bill would remove the North Sea Transition Authority's ability to grant new oil and gas licences. The legislation will not affect the decision on whether to allow drilling at Rosebank off Shetland - the UK's largest known untapped field - which was approved in 2022 before being subject to legal challenges.The UK government said it was upholding Labour's 2024 manifesto vow not to issue licences for new oil and gas fields, as well as underpinning its commitment to reducing global warming. The Conservatives described the bills as "dangerous", accusing Labour ministers of being "totally oblivious the economic and energy threats this country faces". The Energy Independence Bill, if passed at Westminster, would introduce Transitional Energy Certificates, which would allow existing oil and gas fields to provide additional production from "areas bordering or in close proximity to already licensed fields" or in areas that are already part of an existing field. The government said the move could produce about 60 million barrels of oil and support hundreds of jobs.It vowed to sustain "growth and investment across North Sea communities as the energy sector transitions". The wide-ranging bill would also formally scrap gas standing charges and introduce reforms designed to speed up grid connections.The UK government has also announced the establishment of an energy wealth fund using tax revenue from oil and gas extraction, with an initial £2bn of funding, to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "Together, these changes will bring bills down for good, give families greater security and put Britain back in control of its energy future."Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the bill would help to "build a clean energy future which people feel in their pockets, households and communities, ensuring support reaches those who need it most". It comes two weeks after the UK government approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.Ministers said the site, off the coast of Aberdeen, would help heat millions of homes.Environmental campaigners said the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.Both Jackdaw and Rosebank were approved by the previous Conservative government. However, after being subject to legal challenges from environmental groups, Labour ministers have had to decide whether to continue with the projects. Situated 80 miles north-west of Shetland, Rosebank is thought to contain between 300 million to 500 million barrels of oil.Backers say it would be a vital lifeline to the energy industry in the north east of Scotland, and improve energy security at a time when global supply chains are disrupted by conflict. Opponents say it would accelerate the climate crisis, slow down the transition to greener energy sources and do little to improve energy security since its produce would largely be exported overseas to be refined. Greenpeace UK called the bill a "positive step forward for the clean energy transition".However, it called on the UK government to reject Rosebank. Amy McCarthy, the campaign group's head of politics, said: "Saying a resounding no to this oil field - a project that would annihilate every single climate or cost-of-living benefit achieved through this bill - must be step one to securing our power and protecting lives."Aberdeen and Grampian Chamber of Commerce chief executive Russell Borthwick argued that it made "no sense" to wind down North Sea oil and gas production. "Britain will continue to need oil and gas for decades to come," he added."The question is whether we produce more of it here, supporting British jobs, investment and energy security, or pay other countries to produce it for us."David Whitehouse, chief executive of industry body Offshore Energies UK, said the government was right to target energy affordability, but said it should also prioritise energy security. "Today, Britain imports more than 40% of the energy it needs, leaving households and businesses exposed in an increasingly volatile world," he said. "We should be making the most of the energy we produce here at home rather than relying on imports."'Utterly delusional' Shadow Energy Secretary Andrew Bowie, Tory MP for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine, called Labour ministers "utterly delusional".He accused them of being "totally oblivious" to the "economic and energy threats this country faces".Bowie added: "Might as well hang a closed for business sign over Aberdeen and the North Sea."Scotland's First Minister has declined to give a definitive position on whether the UK government should grant the go-ahead for Rosebank.Pressed repeatedly on his position at Holyrood last month, John Swinney told MSPs: "The carbon emissions that come out of the development of an individual site have to be assessed ... as to whether it is compatible with our journey to net zero."That is the legal obligation and that is the test and the assessment the United Kingdom government has got to go through."

schema.headline: UK government to outlaw new North Sea drilling

title: Bowen: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad
description: Donald Trump deals in superlatives, so there is political karma in the sheer size of the defeat handed to him by a big majority of the voters of Ameri
body: Donald Trump deals in superlatives, so there is political karma in the sheer size of the defeat handed to him by a big majority of the voters of America.But do not expect him to go gentle into the political twilight of his career. Losing both houses of the US Congress limits his capacity to dictate, manoeuvre and disrupt at home. Abroad it is likely to be different.As president of the United States and commander-in-chief of its armed forces he retains broad powers to use America's military might.It is not easy to predict the actions and oscillations of Donald Trump. As president, he has turned policy u-turns into weapons. Some things, though, are constants. One is his contempt for those he regards as losers, and his determination never to be seen as one.The president might be tempted to blot out the electoral rout of the midterms by taking actions abroad. He might try to make moves that he can boast about as the decisive and victorious moves of a strong president, undiminished by an election that he insists, despite all the evidence, that was only lost because he was not on the ballot paper.In the weeks leading up to the midterms the deployment of US forces and Trump's own, often belligerent, statements ramped up talk that the US was getting ready to go back to war with Iran. On the eve of the elections, the US carried out a limited bombing raid on an Iranian island in the Gulf.Before he was hospitalised with a stroke, the US Senator Chris Murphy, a Democrat, went to a classified briefing about potential military options for renewed war with Iran.Without going into detail, he condemned the plans as "insane", warning that they would trigger a "devastating escalation". There has been speculation that the Americans have plans to bomb civilian infrastructure. Not only would that be likely to constitute a war crime, it might also be answered by devastating Iranian strikes on equivalent targets on US allies in the Gulf. Its list of potential targets could start with the United Arab Emirates, which is as close to Israel as it is to the US.The regime in Tehran watches political developments in the US closely. It has not concealed its satisfaction that the consequences of its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have become a domestic political issue in the US. Tehran is aware of the damage caused to Trump and the Republicans by the sustained rise in the prices of everything (from petrol and diesel to agricultural fertilisers) caused by the war and its attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.The Speaker of Iran's parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, posted a warning on social media.He said: "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."Benjamin Netanyahu, now acting prime minister of Israel after its election last week, and manoeuvring hard to form a new government, has repeated that he wants to bring down the Islamic regime in Tehran.Reports in Israel and the US say that he is pushing Trump to go back to war.Netanyahu does not have the seats to form a new government with his outgoing coalition.But if a major war restarted and was sustained, and if Israelis came under direct fire, he could have new options of forming a unity government that he would use his considerable political skills to dominate.

schema.headline: Bowen: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad

title: Chris Mason: The US elections will change Trump – how will Burnham react?
description: The first public words from the prime minister after the American midterm elections were instantly revealing about contemporary international politics
body: The first public words from the prime minister after the American midterm elections were instantly revealing about contemporary international politics and diplomacy."Well, President Trump has accepted the results," Andy Burnham said.It is not an observation British leaders have frequently had to make about recent American presidents – that they are not disputing the result of elections in their own country. But what would previously have been taken for granted no longer can be.Burnham remains in the foothills of establishing a relationship with the president – so far it has amounted to a handful of phone calls and one face-to-face meeting at the United Nations in New York in September.As he continues to attempt to build a rapport with Donald Trump, he will be doing so with a president in a wildly different political situation than when Sir Keir Starmer was trying to build bridges with him.No longer is this a story of an extraordinary comeback, but of a midterm president seemingly punished for the consequences of a foreign war the type of which he had originally promised to avoid.And it is noticeable that the British government's public reaction is grounded too in the consequences of the war with Iran: the cost of living."I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all and that's the cost of living," the prime minister said."But I can't get people's cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict between in Ukraine started by Russia."Within government the Iran war and its consequences, particularly on energy prices, is widely seen as the biggest individual contributor among the many factors currently driving up the cost of living.And, bluntly, it is one that puts many, including many of America's allies, in alignment with many in America, Democrat and Republican, who when asked why these elections went as they did, point at the prices displayed outside any petrol station.Speaking before the votes in America were counted, the Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband reflected on this when I spoke to him on BBC Newscast, external.When I asked him specifically if he feared that a domestically humiliated Trump may prove more belligerent internationally, it was to the Iran war the foreign secretary referred.He didn't offer a direct answer to my question, but chose instead to say this: "I know that one of the biggest responsibilities of the whole government, frankly, is the cost of living situation at home, and we know one of the biggest contributors to the cost of living situation is, frankly, the conflict.""The Strait of Hormuz being not exactly closed, but not properly open, not free flowing, and that is hitting families at home," he said."We know that we need a diplomatic way out of this conflict, and so that is one of the things that we're working on. It's something I talked to the U.S. Secretary of State about at the G20, and it's something we continue to work on," he added.The foreign secretary met Marco Rubio at the meeting in Atlanta last week.But the big question for the British government, and so many others, is does defeat at home make it more likely that President Trump gets angrier abroad?Or, do America's traditional allies, the UK, the European Union, Canada, Australia and others feel more strident and willing to work with Donald Trump's domestic political opponents to try to challenge and restrain a weakened president?The answers to these two final questions will determine much in world affairs in the next couple of years.

schema.headline: Chris Mason: The US elections will change Trump – how will Burnham react?

title: Jesus de Miguel: Canary Islands mourn loss of Tenerife forward
description: An island in mourning: Tenerife processes death of De MiguelImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fans have been paying their respects to Tenerife'
body: An island in mourning: Tenerife processes death of De MiguelImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fans have been paying their respects to Tenerife's Jesus de Miguel following his death on TuesdayBySpanish football reporter in TenerifeAs you arrive on the holiday island of Tenerife, there is a profound sense of grief, pain and disbelief at the death of footballer Jesus de Miguel.The Canary island is in mourning for the Tenerife striker, who died from injuries sustained in a collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a match on Monday.The 30-year-old had quickly established himself as a club favourite, scoring 11 goals in his first season as Tenerife were promoted to the second tier of Spanish football.But now the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez Stadium has become a shrine to the player, with hundreds of people gathering throughout the past few days to lay flowers, light candles and pay their respects.Bouquets, rosettes sent by clubs from across Spain, prayer cards, photographs, children's drawings and scarves have been laid around the grounds outside gate nine.It is a deeply moving scene. Fans and residents stand in silence, taking in the tributes.Many are visibly tearful as the scale of the loss begins to sink in at the very place the incident happened.'Football has no colours'Among those paying their respects were Lisa and Lee, visiting Tenerife from Stoke-on-Trent.They had arrived on holiday at the weekend and decided to attend Monday's match, hoping to experience Spanish football for the first time."We never expected something like this to happen," they told BBC Sport."We knew it was serious when the players surrounded him [De Miguel], but to see players crying and actually praying on the pitch was very emotional."When we found out the news the next day, it just really hit us."The couple described the atmosphere inside the stadium as sombre and almost completely silent as spectators waited to understand what was happening."You always expect somebody to pull through," Lee said. "And then seeing the news the next day, it was just unbelievable."They returned to the stadium on Wednesday to lay a Port Vale shirt among the tributes, wanting to show their support for the Tenerife community."Football has no colours," Lisa said. "If it was one of our players, we'd be heartbroken. They're part of your family."Figure caption, Tenerife mourns De Miguel'He's already a legend at the club'For Carlos, a player with Tenerife's disability side Tenerife Foundation, the loss is particularly personal."Honestly, there are no words to describe him. He was incredible," Carlos said as he lay a flag on the ground.He described De Miguel as a figure who had helped shape the club's recent history."He practically gave his heart and soul for the shirt. He's already a legend at the club because, after all, we were in a very difficult position a few years ago and he helped pull us out of it."Without him, I don't think we would be where we are today."Carlos was at Monday's match and said he was left in shock by what unfolded."When I left the stadium I was trembling and I continued to feel that way for hours."Right now, we're incredibly hurt and very sad. I also want to send my support to his family, who I can only imagine must be absolutely devastated."Figure caption, English fans in Tenerife pay tribute to De Miguel'The club is broken. Absolutely heartbroken'The sense of loss has extended far beyond the stadium.Poli Suarez, the Canary Islands' minister for education and sport, said Tenerife was in "complete mourning"."Canarian sport has been left devastated," Suarez told BBC Sport. "The club is broken. Absolutely heartbroken."Suarez also stressed that the thoughts of everyone were with De Miguel's wife, daughter and wider family."They are the ones suffering most directly from this loss, just as the Tenerife supporters are suffering," he said.The government has pledged its support to the club, players and supporters, with Suarez describing De Miguel as a footballer who had become part of the Canary Islands' sporting history."The loss of Jesus de Miguel is now part of our history," Suarez said. "Not only because of the circumstances of his death, but also because of the affection he always showed towards our island and towards his club."A further tribute is planned for Saturday at 18:00 GMT, with supporters encouraged to come together to honour his memory."It will be an opportunity to show our affection and emotion, and to demonstrate our solidarity with the family," Suarez said."We want to show all our affection for Jesus de Miguel."

schema.headline: Jesus de Miguel: Canary Islands mourn loss of Tenerife forward

title: Jesus de Miguel death: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono experiencing 'most difficult days of my life'
description: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.Ten
body: FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono says he is experiencing "the most difficult days of my life" after the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel.Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second division match on Monday.The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all games in European competition this week.Owono's club issued a statement on the goalkeeper's behalf on Wednesday, explaining the 25-year-old "wishes to share a few words personally"."These are the most difficult days of my life," Owono says in the statement."I struggle to find the words, and it is very hard for me to come to terms with what has happened."I feel enormous pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, his family, and everyone who loved him."I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are all experiencing."Rest in peace, Jesus."Earlier on Wednesday, FC Andorra team-mate Lautaro Spatz defended Owono and said he "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and had been "deeply affected" by De Miguel's death.Writing on social media, centre-back Spatz said Owono was devastated.Spatz paid tribute to De Miguel, then said of Owono: "Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone."In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."Players from FC Andorra held a minute's silence before a voluntary training session on Wednesday. Owono was not at the session.Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time on Monday when the incident occurred.Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him, before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.The president of Equatorial Guinea's football federation, Venancio Tomas Micha, issued a statement on Tuesday offering "all our human and professional backing" to the player."As the involuntary protagonist of this tragic incident in the game, he is living through this situation with deep sorrow and distress," he added.On Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell"."Jesus de Miguel's family would like to thank everyone for their messages of support and, from the bottom of their hearts, ask that their privacy be respected at this terrible time. May he rest in peace," added the club statement.Tenerife and Andorra's Spanish second division matches scheduled for the weekend, against Granada and Mallorca respectively, have been postponed.

schema.headline: Jesus de Miguel death: Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono experiencing 'most difficult days of my life'

title: Man Utd: Michael Carrick run has echoes of Jose Mourinho and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer
description: 'Jose Mourinho set to be sacked whatever Manchester United's result vs Newcastle.'As headlines go, it was attention grabbing.Saturday, 6 October 2018.
body: 'Jose Mourinho set to be sacked whatever Manchester United's result vs Newcastle.'As headlines go, it was attention grabbing.Saturday, 6 October 2018.As it turned out, the Mirror was wrong. Although United officials at the time tried to play down the situation, sources have since admitted the intention was to sack Mourinho after presiding over the club's worst start to a season in 29 years, and defeat by Newcastle would make it inevitable. Much like the Roma game, the visitors raced into a two-goal lead and the atmosphere in the stadium started to turn, with most of the venom aimed at the director's box rather than the manager.Mourinho, who had promoted Carrick to assistant coach, replaced Eric Bailly with Juan Mata after 19 minutes and it was Mata who scored the 70th-minute goal that sparked the comeback, completed by Alexis Sanchez in the final minute for a 3-2 victory.After the game, Mourinho said the pressure on him was a "manhunt". However, the relationship between manager and club had been turning sour since the previous summer. His demand for Anthony Martial to be sold had been rejected, while record signing Paul Pogba was proving a problem.While the Newcastle win sparked an improvement in form, a run of two wins in eight games culminating in a 3-1 loss at Liverpool led to Mourinho's dismissal 10 weeks later. Former United defender Rio Ferdinand dismissed calls for Ole Gunnar Solskjaer to be sacked before the Champions League encounter with Atalanta on 20 October 2021 as representative of "current fan culture".Carrick was also part of Solskjaer's coaching group as United went top of the Premier League when they beat Newcastle just over a month earlier, but two wins in seven suggested all was not well.As he did with Roma, coach Gian Piero Gasperini saw his team establish a two-goal lead by half-time, then collapse. Cristiano Ronaldo was the matchwinner on this occasion, nine minutes from time for another 3-2 win.Even if United had lost that night, it is hard to think Solskjaer's job would have been under threat. What followed immediately afterwards was a totally different story.Liverpool came to Old Trafford and established a four-goal first-half lead. Jurgen Klopp's men won 5-0, their biggest ever away win over their old rivals.Many United fans thought Solskjaer should go that night. It was three weeks later that it happened, after a 4-1 defeat at Watford.One look at the Premier League table shows why Carrick is right not to get carried away.If results go against them, Manchester United could be bottom of the table by the time they kick-off against Aston Villa on Sunday.Neither Mourinho nor Solskjaer could follow up their 3-2 successes with another victory. Mourinho's United drew at Chelsea, then lost at home to Juventus. Solskjaer's United were embarrassed by Liverpool. It meant neither man was able to build on the momentum generated by their epic victories.That is Carrick's challenge.United have gone seven Premier League games without a win. They went eight under Ruben Amorim at the end of the 2024-25 campaign, but draws and losses were split by victories en route to the Europa League final, so the effect was not as great as it feels right now.The club does have an exceptional home record against Villa. They have won their past six in all competitions and lost just two league games against the Midlands outfit at Old Trafford since 1983.When United sources finally communicated - almost 48 hours after the 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on 25 October - that Carrick and his players would be given the opportunity to turn the situation around, no timescale was put on this. However, the feeling was the forthcoming international break would be an appropriate time for the club hierarchy to take stock and decide what direction they should go in.In the two games since, Carrick's team have been excellent across two halves.Victory against Villa, albeit with £70m Carlos Baleba joining the injured list, would haul them up to within two points of Unai Emery's side heading into a tricky run of matches post international break, starting at Liverpool, but also including trips to Newcastle and Arsenal in December.Defeat is likely to dump them in the relegation zone for at least a fortnight and facing severe baiting at Anfield on 22 November."It's not about me," is a phrase Carrick has repeated often as he has assessed the wreckage of another bad result. The outcome against Roma was much more positive.There is no suggestion Carrick's future has been decided just yet. What happens at Old Trafford this weekend looks very important.

schema.headline: Man Utd: Michael Carrick run has echoes of Jose Mourinho and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer

title: Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told
description: The banning of Palestine Action has led to a "crisis in confidence" in the UK's anti-terrorism laws and triggered unprecedented civil disobedience fro
body: The banning of Palestine Action has led to a "crisis in confidence" in the UK's anti-terrorism laws and triggered unprecedented civil disobedience from law-abiding protesters, the Supreme Court has been told.Opening a major legal challenge to the group's proscription last year, lawyers for co-founder Huda Ammori said that no other protest organisation had been treated the same way.They told the five justices that the UK's highest court had never before had to consider whether banning a group under terrorism legislation was compatible with freedom of speech and protest.Twenty-seven protesters were arrested outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday as the hearing took place, the Metropolitan Police said.Lawyers for Ammori told the court that thousands of elderly people, many veterans of other radical causes, had been arrested for holding up signs supportive of the group since its proscription.Home Office figures seen by the BBC indicate that there have been more than 4,000 arrests so far at protests in which people have held up signs supportive of the group. In practice, many demonstrators have been arrested more than once, with 1,200 charges authorised by prosecutors to date. Those trials are in limbo until the outcome of this case.Henry Blaxland KC told the court that "far from depriving Palestine Action of the oxygen of publicity" and "far from discrediting its brand", proscription of the group has had the opposite effect."All it's done is to pour fuel on to a fire of one of the most publicly-contested issues of our time," he said."It was disproportionate to do that and in my submission completely unnecessary."During often tense exchanges with the judges, Ammori's team accepted that Palestine Action could not be described as an ordinary and peaceful protest group.They said that its members had carried out "direct action" protests by occupying or vandalising firms linked to Israel's military - with only three of 385 incidents assessed by the Home Secretary as constituting an offence under the Terrorism Act.The UK's definition of terrorism includes incidents of serious damage to property for a cause - and at least two break-ins at defence firms have been described in criminal courts as having caused millions in damage.Raza Husain KC, for Ammori, said that the judges had to put aside allegations of criminality - for which the state had many powers - and consider whether the Home Secretary's decision to label the group as terrorists had been disproportionate."Palestine Action was proscribed on the basis of less than one per cent of its actions over five years assessed as falling within the outer limits of a definition of terrorism," he said."The Home Secretary's own experts confirmed the vast majority of its direct action would not constitute an act of terrorism on the basis that any damage to property is typically more minor. Common tactics include graffiti, petty vandalism, occupation, and lock-ons."One Palestine Action member has been convicted and jailed of fracturing a police officer's back with a sledgehammer - but the court was told that the group had never advocated such violence.The Supreme Court has received arguments from free speech campaigners, arguing the ban interferes with the right to protest.But another submission from a coalition of Jewish groups argued that Palestine Action was a "sinister" organisation intent on attacking its community interests."The Court of Appeal [following earlier hearings] rightly concluded that PA is a violent organisation concerned in terrorism with a wide range of targets," said Adam Wagner KC in written submissions for the Jewish communal groups.He continued: "Its activities are often undertaken covertly with no suggestion of restraint or proportionality, and that at the point it was proscribed it had an escalating trajectory of seriousness and an expanding focus."Wagner said Palestine Action's "crosshairs" had moved from targeting Elbit, a defence firm with an Israeli parent company, to "figures or institutions deemed by PA to be 'Zionist'"."Because most British Jews and Jewish institutions have a connection with Israel, a campaign against institutions PA's activists consider to be 'complicit' with Israel is, in practice, a campaign that threatens the mainstream Jewish community," he said.The case continues on Thursday with a judgment expected at a later date.

schema.headline: Palestine Action ban undermined confidence in anti-terror laws, Supreme Court told

title: All's Fair: Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'
description: "We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is the
body: "We're a full comedy now," the 46-year-old admits, adding: "The beauty in producing a show with writers that are really tuned in to pop culture is they can see what the response is and write accordingly to that."All's Fair, which was created by American Horror Story and Glee showrunner Ryan Murphy, became the Hulu network's most-watched scripted series debut of the last three years and was immediately renewed.Following a group of divorce lawyers - played by Kardashian, Close, Paulson, Naomi Watts and Niecy Nash-Betts - the show was panned for bad acting, with Kardashian bearing the brunt of criticism.The Hollywood Reporter called her "wooden", and the Times declared that the show "may be the worst TV drama ever".But the hallmark of Kardashian's career has been her ability to back herself - whether that's going from years of being snubbed by Met Gala organisers to becoming its most anticipated guest, or overcoming backlash to the launch of her shapewear company to turn it into a $5bn (£3.7bn) brand.Kardashian says: "What is the alternative, right? What is the other choice that you have when you're getting criticised?"Do you just fall in and feel that, or keep your head down and try better, try harder and try a different path?"Having been in the spotlight for more than 20 years, she's "always had a really good sense of my mental health", and says that comes from being able to "brush off" those who seek to bring her down."I always do things that are tough because I genuinely want to learn," Kardashian says.While she was promoting the legal drama last year, Kardashian was waiting to find out if she had passed exams to become a lawyer in real life, after six years of studying for an apprenticeship that negated the need for a university degree.Shortly after the first series aired, she found out she had failed the exam - but says that won't be the end of her pursuit of the qualification."If I don't pass something, if I don't do the best at something, then I'll get there," she says. "I don't worry. I just have to keep going."But after her admission that she had used AI for legal advice, external, she does say she will change how public she is about her studies."I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there," says Kardashian, who has four children with rapper Kanye West and is now in a relationship with British Formula 1 driver Lewis Hamilton. "I know there was a lot of talk out there like, 'she's given up', and that's funny to me. "I like people to think what they want to think and I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," she says.Audiences have only been given a glimpse of what to expect from the second series of All's Fair so far.Co-star Watts, who also serves as a producer on the show alongside Kardashian, says they have "doubled down" on "the high fashion, high drama and heightened reality" that audiences enjoyed the first time around.As for Kardashian's acting, Watts says she's on a "trajectory" that sees her "stepping up in the second season"."She was improvising, riffing, doing all kind of things that I thought were deeply impressive," Watts adds, to which Kardashian jokes: "I think I'm just naturally so funny."One of the positives that critics did cite was the show's desire to spotlight the duality of professional women who were both feminine and successful, which Kardashian says she "loves" because it is "a really realistic depiction of a lot of women I know"."It doesn't mean that just because you're super smart that you can't be fashionable and into glamorous things as well," she adds.

schema.headline: All's Fair: Why Kim Kardashian came back to 'the worst TV drama ever'
